source_read: PMC HTML (PMC2859784; J Stud Alcohol Drugs 2010;71:335-344): abstract, unheaded introduction, Method (Participants, Table 1, Measures, Procedure, Statistical methods), Results (First assessment, Table 2; Change between assessments, Table 3), Discussion, funding footnote.

claims.overstatement: None for the part drawn from this source. The 16th-55th percentile range is the MA group's mean on the five tests that had norms (Trailmaking, FAS, Selective Reminding, Stroop, WCST) in one small, screened sample (27 non-treatment-seeking adults without other drug dependence or psychiatric disorders); it should not be read as describing all users.
claims.note: This source supplies only the percentile range; the 7/27 vs 2/18 and 34% vs 16% figures come from other sources. Qualification worth carrying: on this study's own control comparison several unnormed memory tests and Stroop colour-word showed mean differences of roughly 0.6-0.9 SD (editors' approximation from Table 2 means and SDs: picture recall 0.90, Selective Reminding total 0.67, Stroop colour-word 0.65, word recall 0.61, Stroop colours 0.61, word recognition 0.56), which were not tested individually because the domain MANOVAs (learning/memory p=.09; timed executive p=.09) did not reach .05. 'Normal range on norms' and 'no difference from controls' are therefore different statements.

anchors.extracted: Norms available for Trailmaking, verbal fluency (FAS), Selective Reminding, Stroop and WCST. At the first assessment (4-9 days abstinent) the MA group's mean performance fell in the low-average to average range, 16th-55th percentile; not in the impaired range (authors' example: at or below the 2nd percentile). Authors note similar normative findings in Johanson 2006 and McCann 2008 (Stroop T 43-46) and that the sample was young (early 30s) and otherwise healthy.

27 MA vs 28 controls. Only the attention/processing-speed domain differed (omnibus p<.05); Stroop colours t(53)=2.26, p<.05; composite battery score MA -0.31 (SD 0.45) vs controls 0.01 (0.60), t(53)=2.21, p<.05. Both became non-significant with education as covariate. Learning/memory p=.09 and timed executive p=.09 at domain level; Table 2 shows sizeable mean differences on memory tests that were not individually tested.

claims.overstatement: None. 'About a month' is accurate for the MA group (retest a mean 25.4 days after a first test at a mean 6.2 days of abstinence); controls were retested after a mean 43.5 days. The claim's caution ('not established'; moderate improvement not excluded) matches the data.
claims.note: Editors' calculation reproduced: d = t x sqrt(1/18 + 1/21) = 1.01 x 0.321 = 0.32; SE 0.32; 95% CI -0.31 to 0.96 (Hedges' g 0.32, CI -0.30 to 0.94). Units: the composite change is a mean of change scores each standardized to the control group (the paper reports controls as -0.00), so '0.14 SD' is in control-change SD units, not SDs of test performance. Attrition: 9 of 27 MA and 7 of 28 controls were not retested; MA completers did not differ from dropouts at baseline.

anchors.locator: Results > Change between first and second assessments, final paragraph
anchors.extracted: Standardized composite change: MA 0.14 vs controls -0.00; t(37) = -1.01, p = .33 (18 MA, 21 controls). Across all participants 7 tests improved from first to second session at uncorrected p<.05 (Trails A, three Stroop scores, logical problems, discrimination learning, sentence span), despite alternate forms for most tests. No correlation of MA amount or years with change.

anchors.locator: Results > Change between first and second assessments, para 3; Table 3
anchors.extracted: Domain MANOVAs on change scores: no group differences (all p>.10), also with education, testing interval or estimated IQ as covariates.

Retest interval longer in controls (43.50, SD 15.81 days) than MA (25.44, SD 3.20; p<.01); interval unrelated to change overall and in controls; within MA, longer interval related to more improvement on two tests and less on one (uncorrected). Authors call indications of improvement within one month equivocal and suggest longer abstinence may be needed; they also note differential practice effects could mask or offset change.

claims.overstatement: None relative to this source; the authors themselves say pre- and post-use longitudinal data are needed to establish cause.
claims.note: Users scored lower on average (composite -0.31 SD), groups differed in education and smoking, the differences were not significant after adjustment for education, and change over a month did not differ from controls'. The authors also note education may itself be reduced by drug use, so adjustment may over-correct.

anchors.extracted: MA group had fewer years of education (12.7, SD 1.9 vs 15.1, SD 2.5; t(53)=3.96, p<.01) and more cigarette smokers (21/27 vs 13/28; chi2=6.82, p<.05); no difference in age, sex, ethnicity, mother's education or vocabulary-based premorbid IQ. Composite -0.31 SD and Stroop colours difference non-significant with education as covariate. No relation of years of use or grams/week to composite score.

Authors: premorbid cognitive differences may account for most of the variance rather than methamphetamine-related toxicity, although drug use may also curtail education so adjustment may obscure deficits; longitudinal data before and after use are needed to establish cause.

key_findings.correction: Editors' d recomputed: 2.21 x sqrt(1/27+1/28) = 0.60, 95% CI 0.06 to 1.14.
Editors' d recomputed: 0.32 (95% CI -0.31 to 0.96); Hedges' g 0.32 (-0.30 to 0.94).
Recomputed with 21 vs 18 and weighted pooled SD: word recall 0.82, picture recall 0.81, word recognition 0.79, picture recognition 0.73.

reporting_issues.note: Recomputed from Table 1 counts: sex 0.94 (Yates 0.49), smoking 5.72 (Yates 4.47); ethnicity 0.15 and hepatitis B 0.83 reproduce exactly. Neither printed value (0.34, 6.82) matches either version.
t(50) for vocabulary; Table 2 note gives WCST ns of 13 and 18.

risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-E high overall, driven by confounding (education about 1.1 SD, smoking 78% vs 46%).

interpretation_gap.note: Minor is defensible because the abstract hedges ('considerable') and the Discussion is balanced; the most consequential gap is the abstract's omission that the time-1 differences were not significant after adjusting for education.
